prompt: In `Stop.java`, `main` set `stop = true` and the worker kept spinning. What allowed that?
hint: Nothing said another thread might change the field.

choices.text: A bug in the JIT compiler of Java 25 that later releases will fix
choices.why: It is an optimisation the language permits.

choices.text: `boolean` fields cannot be shared
choices.why: Any field can be shared; this one was shared without a rule.

choices.text: The compiler is free to read the field once
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `sleep(1000)` was too short for the write to happen
choices.why: The write happened: main printed that it did.

prompt: With `-Xint`, the same `Stop.java` ended. What does that show?

choices.text: The interpreter is the correct way to run concurrent programs
choices.why: The program is still wrong; the interpreter just did not expose it.

choices.text: The bug was in the first run's timing only
choices.why: The first run would hang every time once the loop is compiled.

choices.text: Whether it hangs depends on how the JVM runs it
choices.why: Right: why such bugs survive testing.

choices.text: `-Xint` makes every field `volatile`
choices.why: It switches the JIT off; it changes no declarations.

prompt: Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y;` and thread B `y = 1; r2 = x;`. Why is `r1 = 0, r2 = 0` surprising?

choices.text: It means one thread never ran
choices.why: Both wrote their 1; the other just did not see it in time.

choices.text: No interleaving of the four statements produces it
choices.why: Right: it needs a read to pass a write.

choices.text: The arrays start full of ones
choices.why: They start at zero.

choices.text: It means the `CountDownLatch` failed
choices.why: It only started both threads together.

prompt: How many pairs showed `r1=0 r2=0` in the quoted run of `Litmus.java`?
Which statement about reordering holds on every processor?
hint: The numbers change; the rule does not.

choices.text: ARM processors reorder less than x86
choices.why: The other way round.

choices.text: x86 never reorders anything
choices.why: The 0,0 pairs came from an x86.

choices.text: Reordering only happens with arrays
choices.why: Arrays only made it easy to run many tests.

choices.text: Without something ordering them, two threads' accesses have no reliable order
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Match each action with what it happens-before.

pairs.right: the next acquisition of that lock
every later read of that field

right_distractors: every read of any field, in any thread

prompt: `Joined.java` reads a plain `long` written by another thread, and is right every time. Why?
hint: What came between the write and the read?

choices.text: The value fits in a register, so both threads share it
choices.why: Registers are per thread, which is the problem in `Stop.java`.

choices.text: `long` fields are always shared safely
choices.why: Without the `join` it would be a data race.

choices.text: The adder finished before `main` could look
choices.why: Finishing first is timing; visibility needs an edge.

choices.text: `join` creates a happens-before edge
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Two accesses to the same variable in different threads, at least one a write, with no happens-before between them, form a data ___.
One `volatile` write comes after ten ordinary writes in the same thread. Why can a reader of the volatile see all ten?
hint: A happens-before B, B happens-before C.

choices.text: `volatile` makes the whole object volatile
choices.why: It applies to one field.

choices.text: Ordinary writes are always visible immediately; only reads are delayed
choices.why: `Stop.java` showed a write nobody saw.

choices.text: The relation is transitive
choices.why: Right: program order, then the volatile edge.

choices.text: The ten writes are retried until they are seen
choices.why: Nothing is retried.

prompt: Which of these publish an object safely to another thread? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A `volatile` field holding the reference
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: An object whose fields are all `final`
choices.why: Yes, if `this` does not escape the constructor.

choices.text: A plain static field read in a loop
choices.why: No: that is `Stop.java`.

choices.text: Putting it into a `ConcurrentHashMap`
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Calling `System.gc()` after writing it
choices.why: No: the collector creates no happens-before.

prompt: Why can readers of an immutable `PriceList` skip the lock entirely?

choices.text: Nothing in it changes after construction
choices.why: Right; updates replace the whole object.

choices.text: Records are locked by the JVM
choices.why: There is no lock; there is nothing to protect.

choices.text: `List.copyOf` makes the list thread-local
choices.why: It makes the list unmodifiable, which is shared freely.

choices.text: Readers only ever see the first `PriceList`
choices.why: The reader saw the new one, through the `volatile` field.

prompt: Unsafe publication was not reproduced for this course. Why does the lesson still say to follow the rules?

choices.text: Because `final` fields are slower
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: Because the compiler refuses unsafe publication
choices.why: It compiles without a word.

choices.text: Because the bug does reproduce on x86 under load
choices.why: The lesson says it is rare on x86.

choices.text: A bug a test cannot show is still a bug
choices.why: Right: the model, not the run, decides.

prompt: Put the chain that lets `B` see `x = 1` in order, as the figure draws it.
hint: Program order, the edge, program order.

prompt: A colleague fixes `Stop.java` by adding `Thread.sleep(1)` inside the loop, and it stops. Is it fixed?

choices.text: Yes: `sleep` is a happens-before edge
choices.why: `sleep` is not in the list of edges.

choices.text: No: no rule guarantees the worker sees the write
choices.why: Right: it happens to work, which is not the same.

choices.text: Yes, because the loop is no longer hot
choices.why: That explains why it works now, not why it must.

choices.text: No: `sleep` inside a loop is forbidden
choices.why: It is allowed; it just proves nothing.
